# Confidence Intervals
***

The sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies across samples; the *confidence interval* turns knowledge about that sampling distribution into a statement about the unknown parameter.
We will focus on data-driven approaches first, then theory-driven approaches, then theoretical properties of confidence intervals.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
A *confidence interval* is a range of values, computed from the sample, intended to contain the unknown population parameter.

The *coverage* level $1-\alpha$ is the long-run proportion of intervals (constructed from repeated samples by the same procedure) that contain the true parameter.
:::

Confidence intervals are useful for *reporting uncertainty* alongside an estimate: instead of saying only "the mean is $\hat{m}$", we report a range and a coverage level, communicating both the best guess and how much sampling noise could plausibly move it.
The width depends on the sample size, the spread of the data, and the coverage level $1-\alpha$ that the user chooses.


## Resampling Intervals

If we have a sampling distribution for a statistic, the simplest way to read off a confidence interval is to take its middle quantiles.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *critical values* of a sampling distribution are the lower and upper quantiles that bracket the middle $Z\%$ of the distribution.
For a $95\%$ confidence interval, the critical values are the $2.5$th and $97.5$th percentiles.
:::

Critical values are useful because they translate any coverage level into a pair of numbers that can be looked up or simulated, without committing to a parametric model for the sampling distribution.
Often, we have only one sample, in which case we can construct a bootstrap or jackknife sampling distribution (as in [Sampling & Resampling](01_05_Sampling.qmd#resampling-distributions)) and compute the critical values directly from it:

* The $5^{th}$ and $95^{th}$ percentiles are the critical values for the $90\%$ confidence interval.
* The $2.5^{th}$ and $97.5^{th}$ percentiles are the critical values for the $95\%$ confidence interval.
* The $0.5^{th}$ and $99.5^{th}$ percentiles are the critical values for the $99\%$ confidence interval.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x_hat <- USArrests[, 'Murder'] # lab data: murder arrests per 100,000
m_hat <- mean(x_hat)
m_hat
## [1] 7.788

# Bootstrap Distribution
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
boot_means <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means[b] <-m_b_hat
}

# 95% CI
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
boot_ci
##   2.5%  97.5% 
## 6.6039 8.9420

# Visualize
hist(boot_means, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    border=NA, breaks=50)
title('Bootstrap CI', font.main=1)
abline(v=boot_ci)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Using the bootstrap distribution above, here are the $90\%$ and $99\%$ confidence intervals.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 90% CI: 5th and 95th percentiles
quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.05, .95), na.rm=TRUE)
##     5%    95% 
## 6.7998 8.7642

# 99% CI: 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles
quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.005, .995), na.rm=TRUE)
##    0.5%   99.5% 
## 6.20400 9.34002
```
:::

The $99\%$ interval is wider than the $90\%$ interval: demanding higher coverage forces a longer interval.
:::

This approach can be easily extended to other statistics.
For example, a $Z\%$ confidence interval for the median is an interval where $Z\%$ of those generated will contain the population median. 

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
The following code creates a bootstrap CI for the median. 
Edit it to create a jackknife CI instead. 
Then edit it to create a bootstrap CI for the upper quartile. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
med_hat <- quantile(x_hat, probs=0.5) #median
med_hat
##  50% 
## 7.25

# Bootstrap Distribution
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
boot_medians <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_medians)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    med_b_hat <- quantile(x_boot, probs=0.5)
    boot_medians[b] <-med_b_hat
}

# 95% CI
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_medians, probs=c(.025, .975), na.rm=TRUE)
boot_ci
##  2.5% 97.5% 
##  5.85  9.00

# Visualize
hist(boot_medians, freq=FALSE,
    main=NA,
    border=NA, breaks=50)
title('Bootstrap CI', font.main=1)
abline(v=boot_ci)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::

## Normal Approximation

When the sampling distribution is well approximated by a Normal curve, the confidence interval has a simple closed form built from the standard error.

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
The *margin of error* $E$ is the half-width of a Normal-approximation confidence interval, so the interval is $\hat{m} \pm E$.
It equals the critical value times the standard error, $E = q(\alpha/2) \cdot SE(M)$, and shrinks as $n$ grows.
:::

The Normal-approximation interval is useful because it requires only an estimate $\hat{m}$, a standard error $SE(M)$, and a single Normal quantile (no resampling loop, no full sampling distribution).
The $95\%$ interval is the most common and uses critical value $q=1.96$ (the $97.5$th percentile of the standard Normal); the $90\%$ interval uses $q=1.645$.
$SE(M)$ can come from the classical formula $\hat{s}/\sqrt{n}$, the bootstrap, or the jackknife.

A *coverage* level of $1-\alpha$ means that if the same sampling procedure were repeated $100$ times from the same population, approximately $1-\alpha$ percent of the intervals are expected to contain the true population mean.
^[Generally, a coverage level of $1-\alpha$ means $Prob( M - E < \mathbb{E}[X_i] < M + E)=1-\alpha$.
Notice that $Prob( M - E < \mathbb{E}[X_i] < M + E) = Prob( - E < \mathbb{E}[X_i] - M < + E) = Prob( \mathbb{E}[X_i] + E > M > \mathbb{E}[X_i] - E)$.
So if the interval $[\mathbb{E}[X_i] - 10, \mathbb{E}[X_i] + 10]$ contains $95\%$ of all $M$, then the interval $[M-10, M+10]$ will also contain $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$ in $95\%$ of the samples because whenever $M$ is within $10$ of $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$, the value $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$ is also within $10$ of $M$.
But for any particular sample, the interval $[\hat{m}-10, \hat{m}+10]$ either does or does not contain $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$.
Similarly, if you compute $\hat{m}=9$ for your particular sample, a coverage level of $1-\alpha=95\%$ does not mean $Prob(9 - E < \mathbb{E}[X_i] < 9 + E)=95\%$.]

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
For example, suppose we sample $n=36$ monthly electricity bills (in dollars) and find $\hat{m}=142$ and $\hat{s}=30$.
The classical standard error is $SE(M) \approx \hat{s}/\sqrt{n} = 30/\sqrt{36} = 5$.
From theory, we also know that $95\%$ confidence interval has upper and lower critical value of 
$$\begin{aligned}
F^{-1}_{Normal}\left(0.975, SE(M) \right) &= +1.96 \cdot SE(M) \\
F^{-1}_{Normal}\left(0.025, SE(M) \right) &= -1.96 \cdot SE(M)
\end{aligned}$$
Together, we can calculate
$$\begin{aligned}
E &= q(\alpha/2) \cdot SE(M) = 1.96 \cdot 5 = 9.8 \\
[\hat{m} - E, \hat{m} + E] &= [142 - 9.8, 142 + 9.8] = [132.2,~ 151.8].
\end{aligned}$$
We are $95\%$ confident that the population mean electricity bill is between $\$132.20$ and $\$151.80$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_bill_hat <- 142
s_bill_hat <- 30
n <- 36
SE <- s_bill_hat / sqrt(n)
SE
## [1] 5

# 95% CI Manual Calculation
m_bill_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * SE
## [1] 132.2 151.8

## 95% CI Intuition
qnorm( c(0.025, 0.975), m_bill_hat, SE)
## [1] 132.2002 151.7998
```
:::

:::



The main advantages of the Normal approximation is that

* can be computed formulaically as above
* works well for estimating extreme probabilities, where resampling methods tend to be worse.

The main disadvantage is that 

* the sampling distribution might be far from normal.

In the example below, they are all quite similar, but that does not always need to be the case.
The Normal approximation is least reliable when the sample is small or the data are strongly skewed: the sampling distribution is then asymmetric, and a symmetric $\hat{m}\pm E$ interval cannot capture that.
The percentile bootstrap interval reads quantiles directly off the resampling distribution, so it can be lopsided when the data call for it.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Bootstrap Distribution with Percentile CI
hist(boot_means, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 0.7),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
title('Percentile vs Normal 95% CIs', font.main=1)
boot_ci_percentile <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.025, .975))
abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, lty=1)

# Normal Approximation with IID Theory SEs
classic_se <- sd(x_hat)/sqrt(length(x_hat))
x <- seq(5, 10, by=0.01)
fx2 <- dnorm(x, m_hat, classic_se)
lines(x, fx2, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lty=1)
ci_normal <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), m_hat, classic_se)
#ci_normal <- m_hat+c(-1.96, +1.96)*classic_se
abline(v=ci_normal, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lty=3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Note that you can also plug in Bootstrap or Jacknife SEs to the Normal Approximation.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Bootstrap Distribution
hist(boot_means, breaks=25,
    main=NA, border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, ylim=c(0, 0.7),
    xlab=expression(hat(m)^group('(', b, ')')))
abline(v=boot_ci_percentile, lty=1)
title('Percentile vs Normal 95% CIs (with Jackknife SE)', font.main=1)

# Jackknife SE Estimate
n <- length(x_hat)
jack_means <- rep(NA, n)
for(i in seq_along(jack_means)){
    x_jack <- x_hat[-i]
    m_i_hat <- mean(x_jack)
    jack_means[i] <- m_i_hat
}
se_jack <- sd(jack_means)*sqrt(n)

# Normal Approx with Jack SE
x <- seq(5, 10, by=0.01)
fx <- dnorm(x, m_hat, se_jack)
lines(x, fx, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=1)
ci_normal_alt <- qnorm(c(.025, .975), m_hat, se_jack)
abline(v=ci_normal_alt, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lty=3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

Update the example to use `se_boot <- sd(boot_means)` in place of `se_jack`
:::



## Theoretical Properties

A $Z\%$ confidence interval for the mean is an interval where $Z\%$ of the intervals generated on different samples will contain the population mean $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$.
As in [Sampling](01_05_Sampling.qmd#wages-as-a-population), pretend the $3294$ workers in `Wages1` are the whole population, so we know the population mean.
We draw $100$ samples of $n=30$ workers, compute a $90\%$ Normal confidence interval for each, and check which intervals contain the population mean.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Pretend these 3294 hourly wages are the whole population
data(Wages1, package='Ecdat')
population_wages <- Wages1[, 'wage']
population_wage_mean <- mean(population_wages)

n <- 30
n_samples <- 100
sample_CIs <- matrix(nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
for(i in seq(1, n_samples)){
    # Random sample of workers
    x_sim <- sample(population_wages, n, replace=FALSE)
    # Confidence Interval for each sample
    m_sim_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    SE <- sd(x_sim)/sqrt(n)
    CI <- qnorm( c(0.05, 0.95), m_sim_hat, SE)
    sample_CIs[i, ] <- CI
}

# Explicit calculation: whether the population mean is in each CI
covered <- population_wage_mean >= sample_CIs[, 1] & population_wage_mean <= sample_CIs[, 2]
sum(covered) # number of intervals that contain the population mean
## [1] 85

# Visualize confidence intervals
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = range(sample_CIs), ylim = c(0, n_samples))
for(i in seq(1, n_samples) ) {
  col_i <- if (covered[i]) rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3) else rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5)
  segments(
    sample_CIs[i, 1], i,
    sample_CIs[i, 2], i,
    col = col_i, lwd = 2)
}
abline(v = population_wage_mean, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd = 2)
axis(1)
title('90% Coverage (Red = Missed)', font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The count printed above is typically a bit below $90$.
Wages are right-skewed, so with $n=30$ the Normal approximation is not exact, and the long-run coverage of this procedure is closer to $87\%$ than $90\%$.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Here is the same coverage check for uniform random data, where the true mean is $0.5$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n <- 30
n_samples <- 100
sample_CIs <- matrix(nrow=n_samples, ncol=2)
for(i in seq(1, n_samples)){
    # Random Sample
    x_sim <- runif(n)
    # Confidence Interval for each sample
    m_sim_hat <- mean(x_sim)
    SE <- sd(x_sim)/sqrt(n)
    CI <- qnorm( c(0.05, 0.95), m_sim_hat, SE)
    sample_CIs[i, ] <- CI
}


# Explicit calculation: whether the true mean is in each CI
true_mean <- 0.5 # theoretical result for uniform samples
covered <- true_mean >= sample_CIs[, 1] & true_mean <= sample_CIs[, 2]

# Visualize confidence intervals
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = range(sample_CIs), ylim = c(0, n_samples))
for(i in seq(1, n_samples) ) {
  col_i <- if (covered[i]) rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3) else rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.5)
  segments(
    sample_CIs[i, 1], i,
    sample_CIs[i, 2], i,
    col = col_i, lwd = 2)
}
abline(v = true_mean, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd = 2)
axis(1)
title('90% Coverage (Red = Missed)', font.main=1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

We typically have only one sample and compute a single confidence interval with the data we have.
The interval you computed either contains the true mean or it does not.
^[As such, a $Z\%$ confidence interval does not imply a $Z\%$ probability that the true parameter lies within a particular calculated interval.
In practice, people often interpret confidence intervals informally as "showing the uncertainty around our estimate": wider intervals correspond to higher sampling variability and less precise information about $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$.]
So "$Z\%$ confident" translates to "$Z\%$ of intervals constructed on different samples will contain $\mathbb{E}[X_i]$".

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
A confidence interval contains many values, and every one of them is a hypothesis the data cannot rule out.
Suppose a $95\%$ confidence interval for a population mean comes out as $[6.6, 9.0]$.
The data are consistent with $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=7$, and also with $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=8$, and also with $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=8.9$: none of these competing values can be ruled out at the $5\%$ level.
You would, however, rule out $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=5$ and $\mathbb{E}[X_i]=10$, since they fall outside the interval.
"Failing to reject" a value is therefore a weak statement: it says only that the value is one of many still compatible with the data, not that it is correct.
:::

#### **Sampling Distribution Quantiles** {-}

To better understand the link between our theoretical interpretation and our calculations, we will compute the quantiles of the sampling distribution.
E.g., We construct a $90\%$ confidence interval of the mean by taking the $5^{th}$ and $95^{th}$ percentiles of the sampling distribution of the mean.
We draw $300$ samples of $n=50$ workers from the wage population, and then construct a confidence interval using quantiles.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create 300 samples, each with 50 workers
wage_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=50)
for(i in seq(1, nrow(wage_samples))){
    wage_samples[i, ] <- sample(population_wages, 50, replace=FALSE)
}
wage_means <- apply(wage_samples, 1, mean) # mean for each sample (row)

# Middle 90%
mq <- quantile(wage_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the mean is between ', 
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the mean is between 5.09 and 6.63"

hist(wage_means,
    breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.1),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq)
abline(v=population_wage_mean, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8), lwd=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Here is the same calculation for $300$ uniform random samples of size $n=1000$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create 300 samples, each with 1000 random uniform variables
X_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=1000)
for(i in seq(1, nrow(X_samples))){
    X_samples[i, ] <- runif(1000)
}
sample_means <- apply(X_samples, 1, mean) # mean for each sample (row)

# Middle 90%
mq <- quantile(sample_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the mean is between ', 
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the mean is between 0.48 and 0.51"

hist(sample_means,
    breaks=seq(.4, .6, by=.001),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
For another example, consider the median.
We now repeat the above process to estimate the median for each sample, instead of the mean. 

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
## Sample Quantiles (medians)
sample_quants <- apply(wage_samples, 1, quantile, probs=0.5) #quantile for each sample (row)

# Middle 90% of estimates
mq <- quantile(sample_quants, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that the median is between ', 
    round(mq[1], 2), ' and ', round(mq[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that the median is between 4.5 and 6.12"

hist(sample_quants,
    breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.1),
    border=NA, freq=FALSE,
    col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
    main=NA)
title('90% Confidence Interval for the Median', font.main=1)
abline(v=mq)
```

![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}

#### **Interval Size**  {-}

Confidence intervals shrink with more data, as averaging washes out random fluctuations. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create 300 samples of workers, each of size n
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for(n in c(25, 100, 250)){
    # Draw 300 samples
    wage_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=n)
    for(i in seq(1, nrow(wage_samples))){
        wage_samples[i, ] <- sample(population_wages, n, replace=FALSE)
    }

    # Compute means for each sample (row)
    wage_means <- apply(wage_samples, 1, mean)
    # 90% Confidence Interval
    mq <- quantile(wage_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
    hist(wage_means,
        breaks=seq(3, 9, by=.05),
        border=NA, freq=FALSE,
        col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
        main=NA)
    title(paste0('n=', n), font.main=1)
    abline(v=mq)
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
Here is the same comparison for uniform random samples.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Create 300 samples, each of size n
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for(n in c(25, 100, 250)){
    # Simulate 300 samples
    X_samples <- matrix(nrow=300, ncol=n)
    for(i in seq(1, nrow(X_samples))){
        X_samples[i, ] <- runif(n)
    }

    # Compute means for each sample (row)
    sample_means <- apply(X_samples, 1, mean)
    # 90% Confidence Interval
    mq <- quantile(sample_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
    hist(sample_means,
        breaks=seq(.1, .9, by=.005),
        border=NA, freq=FALSE,
        col=rgb(0, 0, 0, .25),
        main=NA)
    title(paste0('n=', n), font.main=1)
    abline(v=mq)
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

Confidence intervals also shrink with lower probabilities of containing the theoretical value.
For a fixed sample size $n$, there is a trade-off between *precision*: the width of a confidence interval, and *accuracy*: the probability that a confidence interval contains the theoretical value.


:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Here is an example showing what a Normal CI estimates. 
Theoretically, $\pm 1 sd$ has 2/3 coverage.
Change to $\pm 2 sd$ to see Precision-Accuracy tradeoff.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Normal CI for each sample
# Uses the last wage_samples above (n=250)
xq <- apply(wage_samples, 1, function(x_row_hat){ #theoretical se's
    mean(x_row_hat) + c(-1, 1)*sd(x_row_hat)/sqrt(length(x_row_hat))
})
# First 3 interval estimates
xq[, c(1, 2, 3)]
##          [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
## [1,] 5.655257 5.308222 5.577791
## [2,] 6.101114 5.703970 6.063878

# Explicit calculation
# Logical vector: whether the population mean is in each CI
covered <- population_wage_mean >= xq[1, ] & population_wage_mean <= xq[2, ]
# Empirical coverage rate
coverage_rate <- mean(covered)
cat(sprintf('Estimated coverage probability: %.2f%%\n', 100 * coverage_rate))
## Estimated coverage probability: 67.33%
```
:::

:::

## Misc. Topics

#### **One-Sided Intervals** {-}

Above, our confidence intervals were two-sided: they contained the middle $Z\%$ of the sampling distribution.
We can also construct one-sided intervals that extend to infinity in one direction.

A one-sided interval is shifted to one side, containing one tail rather than the middle.
For example, an upper-bounded interval uses $(-\infty, q_{0.95}]$, where $q_{0.95}$ is the $95^{\text{th}}$ percentile of the bootstrap distribution: we are $95\%$ confident the true value is at most $q_{0.95}$.
A lower-bounded interval uses $[q_{0.05}, \infty)$, where $q_{0.05}$ is the $5^{\text{th}}$ percentile of the bootstrap distribution: we are $95\%$ confident the true value is at least $q_{0.05}$.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
For the electricity bill example above with $\hat{m}=142$ and $SE=5$, a one-sided $95\%$ upper-bounded confidence interval is
$$(-\infty,~ \hat{m} + 1.645 \times SE] = (-\infty,~ 142 + 1.645 \times 5] = (-\infty,~ 150.2].$$
We are $95\%$ confident the population mean bill is at most $\$150.20$.
Note that $1.645$ is the $95^{\text{th}}$ percentile of the standard normal (compared to $1.96$ for the two-sided case).

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_bill_hat <- 142
SE <- 5
# One-sided 95% upper bound
m_bill_hat + qnorm(0.95) * SE
## [1] 150.2243
```
:::

:::

:::{.callout-tip icon=false collapse="true" title="Test Yourself"}
Here is a bootstrap right-tail example

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Bootstrap Distribution
set.seed(1) # to be replicable
boot_means <- rep(NA, 9999)
for(b in seq_along(boot_means)){
    x_boot <- sample(x_hat, replace=TRUE) # c.f. jackknife
    m_b_hat <- mean(x_boot)
    boot_means[b] <-m_b_hat
}

# One-sided 95% lower bound
# We are 95% confident the mean is at least q_05
hist(boot_means, border=NA, breaks=50,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap')
abline(v=m_hat, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
ci_95 <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(0.05, 1) )
abline(v=ci_95, lwd=2)
```

#### **Prediction Intervals** {-}

Sometimes the question is not "what is the population mean?" but "what range should I expect a single new observation to fall in?".

:::{.callout-important icon=false title="Key Definition" collapse="false"}
A *prediction interval* is a range that aims to contain a future single observation, not a statistic.
We compute it from the lower and upper quantiles of the data themselves, so its width reflects the spread of individual observations rather than the spread of a sampling distribution.
:::

Prediction intervals are useful when the decision depends on individual outcomes rather than averages: forecasting whether a single warranty claim, a single weather day, or a single test score will fall in a tolerable range.
Note that $Z\%$ confidence intervals do not generally cover $Z\%$ of the data.
For the murder rates, compare the $90\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the mean with the middle $90\%$ of the states themselves.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 90% CI for the mean, from the bootstrap distribution above
boot_ci_90 <- quantile(boot_means, probs=c(.05, .95))
boot_ci_90
##     5%    95% 
## 6.7998 8.7642
# Share of states with a murder rate inside the CI for the mean
mean(x_hat >= boot_ci_90[1] & x_hat <= boot_ci_90[2])
## [1] 0.14

# Middle 90% of values: prediction interval
xq0 <- quantile(x_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between ', 
    round(xq0[1], 2), ' and ', round(xq0[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that a new observation will be between 2.14 and 15.4"

hist(x_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 20, by=1), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA,
    xlab='Murder arrests per 100,000')
title('Prediction Interval vs CI for the Mean', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq0)
abline(v=boot_ci_90, col=rgb(1, 0, 0, .8), lty=3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_07_Intervals_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

Only $14\%$ of states have a murder rate inside the $90\%$ confidence interval for the mean, roughly $[6.8, 8.8]$.
The prediction interval, roughly $[2.1, 15.4]$, is much wider because it reflects the spread of individual states rather than the spread of the sample mean.

:::{.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Must Know"}
For uniform random data, the $90\%$ confidence interval for the mean from the quantile example above is roughly $[0.48, 0.52]$, which theoretically covers only a $0.04$ proportion of the data, far less than $0.9$.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x_future_hat <- runif(1000)
# Middle 90% of values
xq0 <- quantile(x_future_hat, probs=c(.05, .95))
paste0('we are 90% confident that a future data point will be between ', 
    round(xq0[1], 2), ' and ', round(xq0[2], 2) )
## [1] "we are 90% confident that a future data point will be between 0.05 and 0.95"

hist(x_future_hat,
    breaks=seq(0, 1, by=.01), border=NA,
    freq=FALSE, main=NA)
title('Prediction Interval', font.main=1)
abline(v=xq0)
```

#### **Recall** {-}

This chapter built *confidence intervals* two ways (the *bootstrap percentile* method and the *Normal approximation*), explained what "$Z\%$ confident" means in repeated sampling, and showed the precision–accuracy trade-off.
The electricity-bill example tied the Normal formula to numbers: with $\hat{m}=142$, $\hat{s}=30$, and $n=36$, the classical standard error is $SE(M) = 30/\sqrt{36} = 5$, and the $95\%$ margin of error is $E = 1.96 \times 5 = 9.8$, giving a confidence interval of $[\$132.20, \$151.80]$.
